items.title: Broadening access to AI for scientists
items.summary: We’re expanding our ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to offer 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to our frontier models.
items.body:
ChatGPT for Academic ResearchersChatGPT for Academic ResearchersChatGPT for Academic Researchers

November 16, 2026 · Research · Science

We’re expanding the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to give up to 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to ChatGPT.

The program began as a pilot in July. Applications for the next round open Monday, November 23. We’ll award 50,000 new grants to eligible researchers on a first-come, first-served basis. Each grant gives the recipient and up to two collaborators free access to ChatGPT Plus. If you’re already on the waitlist and qualify, we’ll email you before applications open with instructions for activating your account.

Participants can use OpenAI’s frontier models and get training on how to use ChatGPT in their research. By default, we don’t use data shared through the program to train our models.

20,000 researchers in 33 countries have joined the program since the pilot began in July. Shuqi Li, a researcher at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, looks for new drug targets that could ultimately shorten tuberculosis treatment. He is exploring whether ChatGPT can help link lab and patient data to speed up antibiotic development. Arthur Porto, assistant curator of AI biodiversity at the Florida Museum of Natural History, and his team uses AI tools to turn photographs of museum specimens into searchable databases. They also created a 3D model of a butterfly whose wings change color as you turn it, just like the real specimen.

We’re also publishing Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT, new research from our Economic Research team examining how more than 1,800 researchers used ChatGPT during the program’s summer pilot. Surveyed participants estimated that, without AI, the same research work at the same quality would have taken nearly twice as long.

We want more researchers to have the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions and make discoveries that improve people’s lives. That is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

The program’s summer pilot helped us understand how researchers use ChatGPT and how we can improve their experience. Based on feedback from researchers, we’re moving away from lottery-based selection. For the next round, we’ll provide access to the first 50,000 applications who meet the eligibility requirements.

The pilot gave researchers access to ChatGPT Pro. When we reviewed pilot usage, we found that most participants would have stayed within ChatGPT Plus usage limits. Based on that finding, we’re offering Plus for new grants so we can extend access to more research teams.

Each grant for this round covers the recipient and up to two collaborators, supporting up to 150,000 researchers. Our goal for the program as a whole is to reach 200,000 researchers, double the goal we announced when the pilot launched in July.

We’ll continue learning from participants about the application process, the capabilities they need, and the support that helps them use these tools in their research. This feedback will help us refine the program and shape future rounds.

Different scientific fields will use AI in different ways, and researchers will need different kinds and levels of support. We’re working with scientific communities to understand those needs and shape our tools, training, and programs around them.

Our support also includes helping scientific communities turn AI-generated results into deeper understanding and new discoveries. In mathematics, we contributed $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative⁠ to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI.

We’re also providing different ways for researchers and institutions to access our tools. ChatGPT for Academic Researchers is just one way we’re helping researchers access advanced AI tools.

• Through ChatGPT Edu⁠(opens in a new window), universities can give their campus communities access to ChatGPT for research, teaching, and learning, with tools for analyzing data and administrative controls for managing access.

• For researchers working in biology, GPT‑Rosalind⁠ brings together specialized biological reasoning and access to scientific tools and databases. The Rosalind Academic Plan⁠ helps bring these capabilities to eligible labs at U.S. universities, offering up to 30 seats at no cost for up to 12 months. Access to GPT‑Rosalind requires approval through our trusted-access process.

Visit our researcher access guide to learn more about ChatGPT Edu, GPT‑Rosalind, and ChatGPT for Academic Researchers.

As these efforts grow, researchers’ experiences will help us understand where our tools are useful, where they fall short, and what support is needed. We’ll use that feedback to improve our programs, develop training and learning resources, and create opportunities for researchers to exchange approaches with one another.

Our goal is to give more researchers the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions—and to keep improving that support as their research and our capabilities evolve.

Learn more about the program⁠(opens in a new window).

items.title: Strengthening the fight against online child sexual abuse with new tools and support
items.summary: New tools, practical guidance, and partnerships will help prevent, detect and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse.
items.body:
November 16, 2026

Safety

Strengthening the fight against online child sexual abuse with new tools and support

New tools, practical guidance, and partnerships will help prevent, detect and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse.

Today, we’re releasing a new tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), interventions that interrupt harmful behavior and point people toward help, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators. These efforts build on our Child Safety Blueprint and our ongoing work to detect, block, and report abuse. For parents, the goal is simple: technology that helps keep children safe, with people in control.

It is well⁠(opens in a new window) established⁠(opens in a new window) that combatting online child predators requires coordination across many organizations. Individual companies like OpenAI have a responsibility to prevent our technology from being exploited by predators to harm children, and we also must work together with the broader industry, child safety organizations and law enforcement to advance our collective efforts to protect children online.

Helping more organizations detect abusive material

We’re building on our current protections with the release of a new image classifier that can detect potential CSAM, including AI-generated material. This new classifier looks for visual signs of abuse, helping teams identify novel images that may not have been seen before. It returns scores that help reviewers decide which images may need attention first. This is the first CSAM classifier with broad availability that has a specific signal on indicating if CSAM may be AI generated.

Our teams trained, evaluated, and designed the classifier for real-world deployment with assistance from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC)⁠(opens in a new window), a nonprofit that operates the CyberTipline, a centralized reporting hub for the online exploitation of children.

We’re offering access to the classifier to vetted organizations through the OpenAI API at no cost, making CSAM detection more accessible to child safety organizations and the broader industry, including those with teams of varying sizes.

Child safety is an industry-wide issue that requires strong collaboration across organizations and a variety of solutions. We’ve engaged the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window) and ROOST⁠(opens in a new window) to help us share access to this new tool, and we are strong supporters of tools developed by others such as Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window) CSAM detection system. In addition, we recently began participating in the Tech Coalition's Lantern program⁠(opens in a new window), where we will share and receive signals relating to online child sexual exploitation and abuse to strengthen cross- platform collaboration.

We’ve tested the classifier internally and with early partners to measure how much abusive material it detects, how often it flags other images, and how it can support safety teams. Their feedback helped us identify weaknesses and improve the system.

Results

Early tests suggest the classifier can help reviewers focus on abusive images while reducing review of false positives. In an evaluation of user-uploaded images, we compared the new classifier with our current protections and found:

• The new classifier could reduce review work: we estimated that it would flag 48% fewer images while finding roughly the same number of abusive images as the existing tool.

• Images flagged by the new classifier were about twice as likely to contain abuse.

Early access partners have also evaluated how the classifier supports their own safety teams. In fal⁠(opens in a new window)’s testing on human-reviewed production images, reviewers confirmed 72% of the classifier’s high-confidence flags as novel CSAM. invideo AI⁠(opens in a new window)’s testing showed one in four flagged cases led to a ban. In SafetyKit⁠(opens in a new window)’s evaluations involving drawings or animations that sexualize children, the classifier detected 90% of cases.

More information about the classifier is available in the CSAM classifier model card⁠(opens in a new window). Organizations interested in the classifier will be able to request access through our intake form⁠. We’ll continue improving the classifier with feedback from those that use it.

Interrupting harmful behavior and pointing people toward help

We already prohibit CSAM, train our models to refuse requests for it, and take action against accounts that violate our policies. We’re building on those safeguards with new product warnings in ChatGPT that interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and point people toward help to stop harmful behavior.

The warning makes clear that sexualizing children causes harm, including when the requested material is AI-generated. Alongside the warning, we’ll remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours, while keeping specialist support available to help people stop harmful behavior. Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions and ultimately account closure or reports to authorities.

We developed this approach with input from organizations and academic advisors that research and develop programs to prevent child sexual abuse, including Protect Children⁠(opens in a new window), the Lucy Faithfull Foundation⁠(opens in a new window), Dr. Caoilte Ó Ciardha, Researcher & Honorary Reader in Forensic Psychology at the University of Kent and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial⁠(opens in a new window) of deterrent messages.

Practical support for developers

The protection of children online doesn’t end with detection. We’ve published CSAM guidance⁠(opens in a new window) to give developers practical steps to prevent abuse, detect harmful content, and act on it. Developed with input from the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window), Thorn⁠(opens in a new window), NCMEC⁠(opens in a new window), and the Internet Watch Foundation⁠(opens in a new window), it is designed for organizations at different stages of building their safety systems.

The guidance provides clear rules, ways for users to report concerns, detection tools, and processes for reviewing and reporting suspected abuse. It also explains how safety identifiers can help developers connect misuse to individual users and how to support the people reviewing sensitive content. Developers can use it alongside tools such as our new image classifier, Moderation API⁠(opens in a new window), ROOST’s self-hosted review console Coop⁠(opens in a new window), and dedicated CSAM detection services such as Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window).

Our commitment to collaboration and supporting the broader developer ecosystem also is reflected in our work with Anthropic and Google to jointly commission new guidance on responding to disclosures of child sexual exploitation and abuse in AI systems. Recently published by the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window), this guidance provides developers with practical recommendations for addressing these sensitive situations.

We’ve already seen this guidance lead to increased numbers of developers accessing child safety tooling and registering to report CSAM to NCMEC.

Supporting child-safety law enforcement units

Protecting children also means supporting the specialist child safety investigators working to find victims and stop abuse. As we’ve discussed publicly with Thorn⁠(opens in a new window), AI can help investigators organize and prioritize information and reduce unnecessary exposure to abusive material.

We’re also supporting child-safety law enforcement units with new tools and trainings on how to use AI in their investigations, including dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. At launch, the first tool will help investigators review lengthy chat logs and legal process returns, identify potential connections, and create timelines, with findings linked to source material.

The initial training is planned as an overview and demonstration, supported by a practical field guide that teams can refer to afterward. It will introduce the tools and how they fit into investigative work. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. Future iterations of the training will be proposed at regional, national and international conferences.

Continuing the work together

These efforts share one goal: preventing harm to children and strengthening the response when abuse occurs. We’ll continue improving our safeguards while empowering child protection organizations, developers, researchers, and investigators with the tools, resources, and expertise they need to protect children, combat exploitation, and bring perpetrators to justice. By working together, we can harness the power of AI to make a meaningful difference in the fight against child sexual exploitation and abuse.

11 月 17 日，据英伟达官方新闻稿，该公司推出 NVIDIA Nemotron for Science，将开源模型 Nemotron 3.5 Super VL、全新开放化学数据集及后训练配方整合在一起，帮助研究人员构建面向科学发现的专用智能体。其中，开放数据集 LitmusBench v0.2 含近 5 万道化学推理题目，数据来源于分子性质与实验药物发现，可用于训练和评估模型对溶解度、人体代谢等分子行为的预测。该模型与数据集现已在 Hugging Face 上线，并针对 128GB NVIDIA DGX Spark 系统做了本地运行优化。

生命科学公司 Lila Sciences、Terray Therapeutics 和 Therna 正在使用并定制该模型。Terray 后训练后用于从科学图表中提取反应物、产物和反应条件，在 RxnScribe 测试中按该基准匹配标准找回约 76% 的标注反应。Lila Sciences 用其设计可执行实验方案，称无需额外微调即可达到与前沿模型相当的表现；结合实验室反馈后训练后，制备量子点的准确率几乎翻倍至 61%，超过 GPT-6 Astra 的 54%，推理成本约为后者的十分之一至二十分之一。Therna 与英伟达合作后训练用于 mRNA 治疗设计，称预测蛋白质表达范围的准确率较前沿模型几乎翻倍，科学家在 96% 的对比中更偏好其解释。

美国能源部阿贡国家实验室正将其整合进 StructBioReasoner 多智能体系统，用于设计和评估癌症等疾病的蛋白质候选疗法，于利希超级计算中心也在接入该模型。瑞典皇家理工学院基于该模型构建了可自行修复损坏 GROMACS 分子动力学设置的智能体，在单台 DGX Spark 上通宵运行并开启推理后，修复了 81% 的测试用例，且均由 GROMACS 独立核验。理化学研究所已通过推理网关 RiVault，在 RIKYU AI 超算平台上提供包括 Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 在内的模型。英伟达超大规模与高性能计算副总裁 Ian Buck 表示，该方案为研究人员提供开源模型、科学数据和后训练配方，以构建能推理科学问题并调用 CUDA-X 加速工具的专用智能体。

OpenAI计划以至少50亿美元价格收购GoodFire

11 月 16 日，据市场消息，OpenAI 计划以至少 50 亿美元的价格收购 GoodFire。

GoodFire（通常写作 Goodfire）是一家专注于机制可解释性（Mechanistic Interpretability）的 AI 研究实验室，核心目标是为大模型做「脑部扫描」，打开 AI 的「黑箱」，让模型的内部决策过程变得可理解、可调试、可控制。它由来自 OpenAI 和 Google DeepMind 可解释性团队的研究人员于 2024 年创立，团队成员大多来自这两家前沿实验室及顶尖高校。其核心技术平台（如 Silico 和 Ember）能让开发者深入模型内部，观察神经元和通路的活动，甚至在训练过程中直接调整参数来改变模型行为，例如已经实现了将大模型幻觉减少一半。

How more than 1,800 scientists used ChatGPT—and what they expect AI to mean for scientific discovery. Explore the findings in our new report.

Download the key takeaways(opens in a new window)Read the full report(opens in a new window)

Scientific progress depends on researchers asking new questions and finding ways to answer them. AI is becoming part of that work, but we’re still learning where it helps and what it could mean for discovery.

OpenAI’s Economic Research team studied more than 580,000 scientific messages from 1,819 scientists in the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers summer pilot and surveyed 251 participants.

Scientists used ChatGPT across the research process, from reviewing literature to analyzing evidence and developing ideas. Surveyed participants estimated that the same work, at the same quality, would have taken 1.9 times as long without AI. And 98% of those who answered our question about discovery timelines expected AI to accelerate discovery in their field.

By default, OpenAI does not use participants’ data from the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to train its models. To protect researchers’ privacy, we used tools called automated classifiers to sort messages by the type of research activity, such as reviewing literature, writing code, or analyzing data. The research team could see those categories, but did not read the underlying messages or ChatGPT’s responses.

We studied how scientists used ChatGPT across the research process.

We looked at how scientists used ChatGPT for ideation. The figures below describe their messages about research ideas.

Led by scientist

35%

of the time, scientists brought a specific question for ChatGPT to work with.

Developed together

of the time, scientists brought an idea and asked ChatGPT to refine it.

of the time, scientists asked ChatGPT to suggest a research question.

6%

The message could not be categorized into one of the other activities.

We asked scientists across different fields to imagine a discovery that would take 10 years without AI and estimate how long it would take with AI.

We measured how often scientists followed up to clarify, check, or revise ChatGPT’s responses across different research activities.

We asked scientists who expected faster discovery to explain why. Three reasons stood out in their answers.

52%

Get research done faster

23%

Find more promising research questions

14%

Pursue a wider range of questions

11%

Other

Scientists could give multiple reasons. Percentages show the share of all 367 reasons identified in 224 written responses.

Scientists in this study used ChatGPT to explore ideas, analyze evidence, write code, and communicate their findings. Their responses also point to ambitions beyond saving time: finding more promising questions and pursuing a wider range of research.

Understanding whether those expectations translate into faster discovery will take more research. Progress will also depend on the funding, staff, and experimental capacity scientists need to test their ideas.

We want to empower more scientists to explore what AI can make possible in their work. Alongside this research, we’re expanding ChatGPT for Academic Researchers⁠, with free access for more than 200,000 researchers around the world. Helping scientists turn their ideas into discoveries that improve lives is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

For more on this study, read the complete paper⁠(opens in a new window) or download the key findings⁠(opens in a new window).

Scientific progress depends on researchers asking new questions and finding ways to answer them. AI is becoming part of that work, but we’re still learning where it helps and what it could mean for discovery.
OpenAI’s Economic Research team studied more than 580,000 scientific messages from 1,819 scientists in the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers summer pilot and surveyed 251 participants.

Scientists used ChatGPT across the research process, from reviewing literature to analyzing evidence and developing ideas. Surveyed participants estimated that the same work, at the same quality, would have taken 1.9 times as long without AI. And 98% of those who answered our question about discovery timelines expected AI to accelerate discovery in their field.

By default, OpenAI does not use participants’ data from the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to train its models. To protect researchers’ privacy, we used tools called automated classifiers to sort messages by the type of research activity, such as reviewing literature, writing code, or analyzing data. The research team could see those categories, but did not read the underlying messages or ChatGPT’s responses.

Scientists in this study used ChatGPT to explore ideas, analyze evidence, write code, and communicate their findings. Their responses also point to ambitions beyond saving time: finding more promising questions and pursuing a wider range of research.

Understanding whether those expectations translate into faster discovery will take more research. Progress will also depend on the funding, staff, and experimental capacity scientists need to test their ideas.

We want to empower more scientists to explore what AI can make possible in their work. Alongside this research, we’re expanding ChatGPT for Academic Researchers⁠, with free access for more than 200,000 researchers around the world. Helping scientists turn their ideas into discoveries that improve lives is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

黄仁勋倒下后，美国商务部长也被查：拖着不收紧芯片管制，儿子的投行还在帮相关企业融资

黄仁勋辞职后，压力开始落到美国商务部长 Howard Lutnick 身上。他目前还在任，但白宫已经在讨论要不要撤换他。

《纽约时报》11 月 15 日又挖出一条重磅线索：Lutnick 一直主张放宽海外数据中心的英伟达芯片限制，而他过去掌管、如今由两个儿子经营的投行 Cantor Fitzgerald，恰好在为相关企业提供金融服务。

其中一家是新加坡公司比特小鹿。它准备在马来西亚建设一座配备英伟达 GB300 芯片的数据中心，预计 2027 年投入运营。知情人士称，这座机房很可能为腾讯提供算力。

比特小鹿已为这座数据中心超过 70% 的算力签下客户合同，预计未来五年收入超过 17 亿美元。Cantor Fitzgerald 与它的合作始于 2024 年，今年又成为其最高 10 亿美元股票发行计划的销售代理之一。

这门生意利用了美国芯片限制留下的空间：中国企业不能直接购买部分顶级英伟达芯片，却仍能租用马来西亚等地的 GPU。芯片不进入中国，企业照样能在海外使用这些算力。

美国政府原本准备收紧这类交易。但《纽约时报》发现，Lutnick 主张只管新加坡、马来西亚等 7 个国家，而且只限制今后出口的芯片，已经建好的机房可以不受新规约束。中国客户用这些算力训练 AI，运营商只需申报，不必一律事先申请许可。

Lutnick 在黄仁勋丑闻中也早已受到质疑。据 Axios 报道，他此前收到过关于黄仁勋与 Alice Huang 关系的机密预警，却迟迟没有对她任职过的英伟达客户 Megaspeed 采取贸易限制措施。

11 月 13 日，美国财政部长 Scott Bessent 公开表示，财政部、国防部、国务院和贸易代表办公室，几个月前就赞成把 Megaspeed 列入出口黑名单，但决定权在商务部手里。

如今，共和党和民主党议员都要求 Lutnick 解释，为什么商务部迟迟没有采取行动。他已同意 12 月 10 日赴国会作证。11 月 16 日，民主党参议员 Maria Cantwell 又致函指责商务部未能堵住芯片管制漏洞。

美国商务部否认 Lutnick 的政策受到家族生意影响，称他已转让相关持股，也不会与儿子讨论部门事务。

特斯拉自动驾驶团队出走创业：估值11亿美元，专门给机器人造虚拟世界

三名特斯拉自动驾驶仿真团队前负责人创办的 Zeromatter 正式亮相，估值达到 11 亿美元，累计融资 1.6 亿美元。公司已有超过 130 名员工，其中约 40 人也来自特斯拉。

三名创始人此前都是游戏开发者。CEO Ian Glow 曾参与开发 Minecraft，后来带领特斯拉的仿真团队，为自动驾驶和 Optimus 人形机器人搭建虚拟测试环境。

Zeromatter 把这套技术做成了独立产品。客户可以在虚拟世界里训练自动驾驶汽车、无人机和机器人，反复测试危险或罕见场景。比如模拟儿童突然从停放的汽车后方冲出，或者让机器人尝试抓取、安装零件，不必在现实中冒险。

它的重点是让模拟结果尽可能接近现实。公司自研了物理引擎和传感器模拟系统，不仅要还原画面，还要模拟碰撞、摩擦、摄像头误差等细节。团队会购买真实设备，在实验室测量各种情况，再与虚拟结果逐一比较。

Glow 认为，机器人走路、跑步已经取得很大进展，真正困难的是让双手准确操作物体。Zeromatter 正在重点攻克这类需要精确模拟接触和摩擦的任务。

特朗普拟选20多家AI「国家冠军」：英伟达、OpenAI、Anthropic都在名单上

特朗普政府准备把英伟达、亚马逊、微软、OpenAI、Anthropic 等 20 多家公司列为美国 AI「国家冠军」，帮助它们到海外抢生意，与中国科技企业竞争。

入选后能得到什么好处？美国政府会帮这些公司向外国政府推销产品、协调海外项目，还能优先审查芯片等技术的出口许可证，并协助申请联邦融资。

美国还打算把芯片、数据中心、AI 模型和应用软件打包出售。比如外国政府要建设 AI 数据中心，可以直接采购一整套美国技术，不必分别寻找芯片厂商、云服务商和模型公司。

这项计划早在 2025 年 7 月就已启动。今年 7 月，美国商务部称收到 78 份申请，涉及从芯片到 AI 应用的整套出口方案。这次准备公布的是重点扶持名单，预计由商务部长 Howard Lutnick 在未来一周宣布。

谷歌 Antigravity 负责人 Varun Mohan 宣布，Antigravity 已将 Gemini 4 Argon、Carbon、Hydrogen 三款模型的上下文窗口扩大一倍。每轮对话触发的上下文压缩次数可减少约 3.5 倍，让 Agent 在长任务中少花时间整理历史信息。

Varun 还透露，Antigravity 即将加入原生电脑操作（Computer Use）功能，让 Agent 能够直接操作桌面软件。

不少开发者在 Varun 和 Google DeepMind 的 Gemini 后训练负责人 Melvin Johnson 的评论区抱怨，Carbon 虽然能力很强，但运行速度太慢。Melvin 承认正在提速，并透露团队已有兼顾速度与模型能力的方案。Varun 则表示，此次上下文扩容也能减少压缩耗时，加快任务完成。

有用户希望推出每月 300 美元、500 美元的更高额度套餐，Varun 回复称「正在做」。Melvin 还透露，Antigravity 移动 App 已在规划当中。

过去一周，Antigravity 还接连上线 Gemini 4 Carbon、Hydrogen 两款模型，推出 Swarm 多 Agent 并行协作、Orchestrator 不同模型分工，以及用 Python 编排 Agent 任务的 Dynamic Workflows。

items.title: How Revolut raises ambition without lowering the bar
items.summary: Discover how Revolut uses OpenAI models and Codex to cut coding time by 30–60%, scale financial crime investigations, and innovate without compromising security.
items.body:
November 16, 2026

With OpenAI models and Codex, Revolut is giving its teams more room to solve complex problems—from software engineering to financial crime.

Contact sales

Company size: Enterprise

Region: Global

Industry: Technology, Finance

Products: ChatGPT, API, Codex

30–60%

Reduction in coding time from task start to feature merge

One day

To turn seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context

1–2 days

Saved on security code review with Codex

Revolut⁠(opens in a new window) was built to challenge the way people interact with money. That ambition now stretches across more than 40 markets, 800,000 businesses and a consumer base that’s grown by 23% in the last 12 months.

Add to that a company culture that expects small, lean teams to move quickly and it’s no surprise that ChatGPT and Codex have proven a natural fit.

“The perfect description for a high-caliber Revolut person is someone who can identify a problem really quickly, deduce the solution, design four scenarios, identify the best one of those four then take it to market,” says Kim Maniovich, Revolut’s Global Head of Business Marketing.

“Partnering with OpenAI enables us to build a lot of these solutions in a way that’s incredibly lean, cost-efficient and really tailored to the unique way that we work.”

But moving faster is only part of the opportunity. For Revolut, the bigger question is what becomes possible when talented people spend less time on the mechanics of getting things done—and more time tackling problems that could fundamentally change financial services.

As Revolut grows, so does the complexity of protecting its customers. According to one report⁠(opens in a new window), over half of adults worldwide reported a scam encounter in 2025.

For Revolut, every transaction creates another opportunity to identify suspicious activity, investigate potential risks and implement robust and tailored protections for its customers. But the sheer volume of those transactions far outstrips the human resources available to any bank.

“The biggest problem we can tackle with AI today is the scaling of humans versus the demand that we get,” says AI Lead David Abitbol. That’s why one of Revolut’s largest AI applications is a FinCrime agent powered by OpenAI models.

Rather than requiring investigators to work through every eligible case manually, the agent can examine information, apply Revolut’s rules and complete the defined process automatically.

The release of GPT‑5.5 was a turning point. It was then, says Abitbol, that the models had become capable and cost-effective enough for Revolut to delegate screening and investigation workflows entirely to the agent. The result is greater capacity to monitor transactions without increasing investigator headcount at the same rate as demand.

That, adds Information Security Engineer Mo Amiri, “translates directly into stronger protection and a more resilient system our customers can trust.”

‘Move fast but build trust’ could easily be Revolut’s internal engineering slogan. While Abitbol points out that Codex has delivered a 30-60% reduction in coding time, he’s also clear that certain guardrails are non-negotiable.

“We have a systematic framework where anyone in the company who’s building anything with AI has the same set of standards across development, A/B testing, and business metric prediction,” he says. “So every engineer is held to the same standard of quality across the company. We started to get enough intelligence for reasonable costs where we could increasingly delegate initial investigations and screenings to the agent.”

For Senior Platform Engineer Dmitry Pitik, that 30-60% reduction in coding time became tangible while he was building an internal code-review service. He designed the system, broke it into features and initially assumed he’d need a development team to implement it.

“I realised I don’t need a whole team of developers to implement this,” he recalls. “I can just launch different agents and assign each of them a particular task.” Codex became his implementation team, while Dmitry spent more time designing the system, planning the work and reviewing what came back.

This is a pattern that Abitbol has seen across Revolut. As Codex returns capacity to engineers they’re using that reclaimed time “to spend more time discussing design and the best solution. So we spend more time designing instead of implementing.”

That doesn’t remove the need for engineering expertise, it just changes where that expertise is applied. “Every developer is responsible for the code they produce, and we don’t blindly trust AI,” Pitik says. The result is a different division of work: AI can help with implementation, while engineers devote more attention to the decisions that determine whether the software is useful, reliable and worth building.

That overhead is worth it. As Codex works on one task, Pitik can work in parallel on another. That kind of multitasking is essential in a company where, as Kim Maniovich explains, the average employee has “three different jobs.” Using Codex creates a virtuous (if challenging) flywheel where “month on month the targets we’re setting get more aggressive, but also more attainable. And so the bar keeps moving up. AI is making that possible.”

Examples of what Revolut has been able to do with this new-found capacity include developing a tool to build web UIs for internal apps and external-facing products.

Or turning seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context in a single day, creating a foundation for tools intended to help designers work more effectively. The exercise illustrates how AI can make accumulated organisational knowledge more accessible, reducing the effort required to work with complex systems. “We can shift focus from the things which are important but hard to do without AI to the things which matter for customers,” says Senior Designer Dmytro Pavlov.

“I realised I don’t need a whole team of developers. I can just launch different agents and assign them a task.”

—Dmitry Pitik, Senior Platform Engineer, Revolut

Mo Amiri’s job is to make sure all of this speed is matched by security—not just for customers but for Revolut’s own employees. That gives him two views of AI at once: how it can help Revolut investigate a problem, and what teams need before they can deploy it safely.

In a phishing investigation, for example, an analyst once had to gather an email, inspect its links and attachments, trace the sender and assemble the evidence manually. “With stronger AI tools, we can uncover those connections instantly, and dig deeper into the questions that really matter,” he says.

While AI does the legwork and presents an investigator with a structured case, it’s still down to the individual to review the original records, decide whether the explanation makes sense and approve any action.

Amiri applies the same thinking when teams bring new AI applications into Revolut. He follows the complete chain: what information the system sees, where that information goes, which tools it can reach, what it can do with that access and what happens when something fails. He also tests whether apparently convincing conclusions are actually supported by the evidence.

“The most critical decision is always about accountability,” he says. “If an AI tool suggests a code change, a human engineer needs to understand that change well enough to stand by it. That directly drives how we design the review process, giving developers the context they need without cluttering their everyday workflow.”

For Revolut, safeguards aren’t separate from innovation. They help establish the conditions under which teams can confidently adopt more capable technology. “That’s how you earn real confidence in AI,” he explains, “by making thoughtful decisions upfront and testing as you go.”

“You earn real confidence in AI by making thoughtful decisions upfront and testing as you go.”

—Mo Amiri, Information Security Engineer, Revolut

• 30–60% reduction in coding time from task start to feature merge

• One engineer built an internal code-review service by delegating implementation tasks to multiple Codex agents

• One day to transform existing design-system documentation developed over roughly seven years into AI-readable context

• One to two days saved on one substantial security code-review task

• More transactions screened through the FinCrime agent without scaling investigators one for one

• Start with a problem worth solving. Revolut has put AI to work where demand is growing fastest and the stakes for customers are highest.

• Use speed to raise ambition, not lower standards. Time saved on coding and investigation creates room for better design, harder questions and more consequential work.

• Keep people on the hook. AI can gather evidence, write code and recommend action. A person still needs to understand the work well enough to stand behind it.

• Build trust before you scale. Be clear about what a system can see, what it can do and what happens when it fails—then test those decisions as you go.

• Make your knowledge usable. AI works better when it can reach clear, well-organised context. The same exercise often shows where the organisation itself needs to be clearer.

Revolut has already shown how AI can increase the amount and complexity of work its teams can attempt. Its next opportunity is to carry that combination of capability, judgment and design into the way customers interact with their money.

Abitbol imagines a more conversational interface in which customers can ask Revolut to help with everyday financial tasks: blocking a card, managing a subscription or finding ways to save for a trip. Pavlov sees the design challenge underneath that experience—turning complexity into something consistent, familiar and easy to use.

Kim Maniovich connects that future to the culture driving the work. “I hope that we can take the values that we operate by every day—this unapologetic ambition, the desire to never settle—and enable people to apply that to their own lives through the products that we build for them.”

As AI makes it easier to build, the differentiator becomes knowing what to build—and maintaining the judgment, standards and customer understanding to do it well. For Revolut, that’s the bigger promise of intelligence at work: less time spent on the mechanics of getting things done, and more capacity to make financial services safer, simpler and more useful for everyone.

乌兰察布AI基建有多疯狂：25GW算力项目已签约，近3万人同时赶工

前段时间，美国研究机构 SemiAnalysis 专程来到内蒙古乌兰察布，将规划 800MW 的远景星河基地称为「中国版 Stargate」。然而，这座足以与美国超大型 AI 数据中心相提并论的园区，在乌兰察布只能算冰山一角。一场规模更加庞大的算力建设，正在这片草原上铺开。

根据当地公开数据，截至今年 10 月中旬，乌兰察布累计签约 109 个算力中心项目，签约 IT 供电容量超过 25GW，规划机架规模超过 700 万架。

《晚点》记者近期在乌兰察布实地走访了 72 小时。当地察哈尔高新区就有 22 个算力项目同时施工，近 3 万名工人在不同工地赶工。

在巴音片区，十几辆几十米长的板车排成一排，运载着数百个尚未拆封的服务器机柜。道路两侧有 4 个数据中心同时建设，到了晚上，塔吊和挖掘机还在施工。一些工地每三个月就要完成一栋机房楼。

客户要求的交付时间也越来越短。远景 AI 智算中心 CTO 胡兴赞透露，过去客户能接受 12 个月的建设周期，后来缩短到 9 个月、6 个月，现在甚至要求两三个月交付。

因为 GPU 太贵，机房延期一天，就可能让价值数十亿元的计算设备继续闲置。一名项目负责人透露，如果未能按合同交付机房，每晚一天就要赔偿客户 50 万元，一个月就是 1500 万元。

为了赶工，建设方开始提前拿地、建设厂房、采购大型设备。部分配电系统直接在工厂组装成模块，运到现场后再连接。原本需要 10 天的安装工作，可以压缩到 2 天。

马化腾讲话引争议后，腾讯官方发文：AI时代不一定要那么多管理岗位，别占着地盘不动

11 月 16 日，腾讯文化正式公布 28 周年总办 LinkTime 现场笔记。相比上周流出的马化腾讲话，这次把组织改革的矛头指得更清楚。

总办直言，未来不一定需要那么多管理岗位。那些只负责中间传话、不愿改变还占着位置的干部，不能再成为公司转型的阻碍。各部门的山头主义、地盘意识都要打破。

腾讯还承认，不少基层员工很有动力使用 AI，也愿意做出新东西，却被旧有的组织架构限制住了。公司希望减少管理层级，让更多小团队直接开展工作。

重新组建混元团队也让腾讯意识到，团队能力不能只靠少数顶尖人才。其他成员的水平能不能一起提高，同样重要。如今游戏、金融、安全等团队也开始参与混元模型的共同设计。

上周马化腾在全员会上强调，转型不能再靠哄、靠谈条件。这次官方笔记进一步提出，连过去设置的管理岗位和部门边界，都要重新审视。
